header:
Date: 2026-05-14
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Location: Zoom (recording enabled)
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Victor Alvarez (Redwood SE), Jordan Mills (CardinalPath - Head of ML), Sofia Ruiz (CardinalPath - Platform Eng), Evan Park (CardinalPath - CTO)
summary: SE-led console deep dive focused on request playback, trace mapping, and error-forensics. CardinalPath wants to validate Redwood's ability to reproduce failing inference requests, map error paths across model fallbacks, and review security/compliance constraints for a short pilot. Action: Redwood to send security excerpts and run a 2-hour pilot with three provided request IDs.
transcript:
[15:30] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We'll run through the request playback flow in the Console and then dig into error mapping and fallbacks. Victor will drive demo.
[15:31] Jordan Mills: Thanks, Maya. Quick context — we're seeing intermittent 5xxs in production, usually at tails of long chats, and sometimes cost spikes when requests re-route. Goal here is to see if we can reproduce and map them end-to-end.
[15:32] Victor Alvarez: Got it. Can you confirm where you run inference today — hosted endpoints, self-hosted, a mixture?
[15:32] Sofia Ruiz: We're on a mix. Most prod traffic goes to a managed endpoint on AWS, some experimental workloads on-prem for PHI data. We want VPC peering and KMS integration for the pilot.
[15:33] Evan Park: Timeline is tight — we'd like a pilot in the next week, success criteria are reproducible playbacks for 3 failures and latency staying < 150ms p50 for short queries.
[15:34] Maya Chen: Quick note — Redwood's private mode supports customer-managed VPC and KMS/HSM. We'll include the security cheat sheet.
[15:35] Victor Alvarez: I'll share the runbook. Alright demo — opening Console -> Requests -> filter by status -> we'll pick a failed request. (screen noise) Sorry, that was a notification.
[15:36] Victor Alvarez: 15:36 — selecting request ID 7f9a3c. On the right pane we have metadata: model variant, node ID, latency breakdown. Sometimes the transcription of the node name shows as 'node zero' or 'noad-0' in the export — the speech-to-text can garble.
[15:37] Jordan Mills: That metadata looks promising. Does the Console show KV cache hits? We suspect cache staleness causing divergence.
[15:37] Victor Alvarez: Yes — under 'runtime hints' you can see KV cache metrics: prefix hits, marginal reuse. For this request we have 0 prefix hits and a large kv-miss penalty at token 1-10.
[15:38] Sofia Ruiz: Can you show the exact token-level latencies? We need to correlate to our app logs.
[15:38] Victor Alvarez: Sure — expanding 'token timeline'... there's a spike around token 18 where the kernel fell back to a slower quantized path. The Console marks that as "kernel fallback" and you can drill into the kernel selection history.
[15:39] Maya Chen: Quick clarification — the kernel fallback can happen when sequence length crosses thresholds or memory pressure occurs; we can tune quantization / batch profiles in Optimize.
[15:40] Evan Park: What about model routing? If the main model is overloaded do requests automatically route to a cheaper variant? That's a concern for quality.
[15:40] Victor Alvarez: By default routing policy is latency-first with automatic fallback to compatible model variants in same family. You can set policy to cost-first or strict pinning to avoid silent fallbacks. Console shows the routing trace: original route -> fallback route -> response.
[15:41] Jordan Mills: I want that trace. If we can link the Console request-playback to our app's request ID and show the exact model variant used, that solves half our problem.
[15:42] Victor Alvarez: That's what request correlator does — there's a link between the app request ID (if you pass x-request-id) and Redwood's internal request. In the playback you can step through each micro-call and see which model shard handled it.
[15:43] Sofia Ruiz: There's been talk about the audit logs and retention. How long do you keep full trace payloads, and can we restrict retention per-route?
[15:43] Maya Chen: We default to 30 days for full payloads on hosted plans, longer for enterprise with S3 export. You can set per-route retention in Console and enable partial redaction. We'll send the exact policy excerpts.
[15:44] Evan Park: What about encryption in transit and at rest? KMS key rotation?
[15:44] Maya Chen: We support customer-managed KMS for private deployments; hosted has envelope encryption with rotation policies. We'll attach the security doc.
[15:45] Victor Alvarez: Back to the playback — I'm going to use the playback scrubber. At 00:00:12 you can see a call to the tokenizer, then the model step, then a fallback. The 'failing block' shows an exception: OOM on node 3, then automatic fallback to quantized-8bit variant. Transcription sometimes shows as "O O M" or "oh oh em" in the auto notes.
[15:46] Jordan Mills: So OOM triggers fallback — can we force a retry versus fallback? We prefer retrying on a warmed cache before switching models.
[15:46] Victor Alvarez: Yes, retry policies are configurable. We have canary/gradual rollouts and a retry-with-kv-refresh option. That option attempts a lightweight warm call to prime caches before fallback.
[15:47] Sofia Ruiz: Is that configurable per-route? We'd like to enable it only for chat routes.
[15:47] Victor Alvarez: Absolutely, per-route policies in routing -> advanced. We'll show that in the runbook.
[15:48] Maya Chen: Quick aside on observability: the Console exposes token-level cost and you can backfill cost to traces for chargeback. Also you can create alert rules on spike patterns.
[15:49] Victor Alvarez: I'll export a sample trace now. (short pause) Export complete — attaching download link in the chat: https://redwood.example/runbook/sample-trace-7f9a3c.json (link placeholder). Note: sometimes the link text in auto-transcript omits dashes.
[15:50] Jordan Mills: Nice. I see fields for model_hint, kernel_path, node_id, kv_stats. This will let us map to our side.
[15:51] Evan Park: A question on latency targets. You mentioned p50 150ms earlier — we need SLOs and SLA language. Is that in the dedicated or hosted offering?
[15:51] Maya Chen: Dedicated gives most predictable latency with reserved GPUs and capacity commitments; hosted can hit low latency but without reserved pool you'll see higher variance. We'll include the SLA excerpts.
[15:52] Sofia Ruiz: One more — for pilot scope, can we run a short bench with their three failing IDs and a small synthetic load? We want to see both reproduction and cost delta with and without retry/warm policies.
[15:52] Victor Alvarez: Yes, we typically run a 2-hour pilot bench where we replay the provided requests at controlled concurrency and collect traces. We'll correlate them to your app IDs.
[15:53] Jordan Mills: Perfect. Any blockers on our side? We'll need a secure upload for the anonymized payloads.
[15:54] Maya Chen: We'll provide a pre-signed S3 link and an upload checklist (redaction guidance). Also we'll send the minimal network requirements for VPC peering.
[15:54] Evan Park: Sounds good.
[15:55] Maya Chen: Recap: Redwood to send security/retention excerpts, Victor to share runbook and sample trace, CardinalPath to provide three request IDs + payloads; schedule pilot for next week. Anything else?
[15:56] Jordan Mills: No, that's it. Thanks all.
[15:56] Maya Chen: Thanks, everyone. We'll follow up with docs and calendar invite.
[15:56] (recording ends)
